2743: Aramaic or Hebrew original (fragments of four Aramaic copies and one Hebrew copy found at Qumran, 4Q196-200); survives complete in two Greek forms (short and long) and in Latin.
2744: A Jewish author, probably in the Diaspora (eastern Mediterranean or Mesopotamia) or possibly Judea; the story is set among Israelite exiles in Nineveh after 722 BC.
2745:
Tobit is a short, carefully told family story. Tobit, a devout Israelite of the tribe of Naphtali deported to Nineveh, buries executed fellow Jews at the risk of his life, is blinded by bird droppings and prays to die. Far away in Ecbatana, a young relative named Sarah has lost seven husbands on their wedding nights to the demon Asmodeus and also prays to die. God sends the angel Raphael, disguised as a kinsman, to guide Tobit's son Tobias on a journey: a fish caught in the Tigris yields the cure for both troubles, Tobias marries Sarah, and Tobit's sight is restored.

The book is a showcase of Diaspora piety: almsgiving, prayer, fasting, burial of the dead, marrying within one's people, honouring parents and keeping faith far from Jerusalem. Tobit's farewell speeches (chapters 4 and 14) contain a negative form of the Golden Rule and the hope that Jerusalem and the Temple will be rebuilt in glory. Historians note that the story compresses or confuses some Assyrian history (for example it makes Sennacherib the son of Shalmaneser, when his father was Sargon II, and has Tobit alive from the division of the kingdom to the fall of Nineveh). Many readers, Catholic scholars included, therefore read it as an edifying tale rather than a chronicle.
2746: A family story about a blind, faithful Jew in exile, his son's journey with a disguised angel, and a bride freed from a demon. It teaches prayer, generosity and trust in God's hidden care. Catholics and Orthodox count it as Scripture; Jews and most Protestants do not.
2747: Tobit's good deeds and blindness in Nineveh (ch. 1-3)
2748: Sarah's plight in Ecbatana and the two prayers heard together (ch. 3)
2749: Tobit's instructions to his son, including almsgiving and the negative Golden Rule (ch. 4)
2750: Journey with Raphael, the fish, marriage to Sarah and the demon driven off (ch. 5-9)
2751: Homecoming and healing of Tobit's eyes; Raphael reveals himself as one of seven angels (ch. 10-12)
2752: Tobit's hymn and final prophecy of a rebuilt Jerusalem (ch. 13-14)
2757:
Jews: Tobit was never part of the Hebrew Bible. Rabbinic tradition held that the books defiling the hands (that is, sacred) were closed, and Tobit circulated mainly in Greek. The Qumran finds show Jews did read it in Aramaic and Hebrew before AD 70, so the exclusion was not because no Semitic original existed.

Protestants: the Reformers followed Jerome's *Hebraica veritas* (Hebrew truth) principle: the Old Testament canon is the Hebrew Bible the Jews kept. They also pointed to historical difficulties (the Assyrian king list, Tobit's improbable life span), to Raphael's fish-liver smoke against a demon (which seemed magical to them), and to the teaching that almsgiving purges sin (Tob 12:9), which they saw as clashing with justification by faith. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles lets it be read for example of life but not for doctrine; the Westminster Confession gives it no authority.
2758:
Catholics and Orthodox note that Tobit was in the Greek Old Testament used by most early Christians, was read and cited by Fathers such as Polycarp, Cyprian and Augustine, and appears in the lists of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397). Trent (1546) and Jerusalem (1672) confirmed it. The Ethiopian and Syriac churches also keep it.

Its defenders value it as a theology of everyday faithfulness: God works through ordinary events and hidden angels, prayer is answered, marriage is holy (Tobias's wedding-night prayer is still read at Catholic weddings), and charity matters. Raphael's statement that he is one of seven angels who stand before God is echoed in Revelation, and almsgiving language resembles that of Jesus. On the historical slips, Catholic scholars often answer that the book's genre is a didactic story, so its truth does not depend on Assyrian chronology.
2760: An Old Testament-era book, so apostolic authorship does not apply; no apostle names it.
2762: Composed c. 225-175 BC, after the prophets in the Jewish view (Josephus held that prophetic succession ended with Artaxerxes), but early enough to be copied at Qumran.
2764: Its piety is fully Jewish and mostly uncontroversial; Protestants object to almsgiving that purges sin (Tob 12:9) and the angelic exorcism.
2766: Widely used in the Greek-speaking and Latin churches, but excluded by Jews and by some Fathers who followed the Hebrew list (Jerome, Athanasius).
2768: Read in church from early times; quoted by Polycarp and Cyprian; used in marriage liturgies.
2770: Makes no claim to be prophecy; it presents itself as Tobit's own memoir and story.
2771: Echoes Tobit's teaching that almsgiving delivers from death.
2772: Quotes Tobit repeatedly in urging generous giving.
2773: Placed it among books not in the canon but appointed by the Fathers to be read by new converts (with Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the Didache and the Shepherd).
2774: Said the Church reads Judith, Tobit and the Maccabees (and Wisdom and Sirach) for edification but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures or use them to prove doctrine.
2776: Its canon list (preserved in the Breviary of Hippo) counts this among the books to be read in church as divine Scripture.
2778: Repeated the Hippo list of canonical Scriptures, which includes this book (as part of the wider Greek Old Testament).
2780: Defined this book as sacred and canonical for Catholics, with anathema for those who knowingly reject it.
2782: Under Patriarch Dositheus, named this among the books it calls genuine parts of Scripture, against Protestant-leaning statements attributed to Cyril Lucaris.
2784: Article VI names it among the books the Church reads for example of life and instruction in manners, but does not use to establish doctrine (citing Jerome).
2786: Says the books commonly called Apocrypha are not divinely inspired, are no part of the canon, and carry no more authority than other human writings.
2787: Jesus gives the positive Golden Rule; Tobit 4:15 has the negative form (what you hate, do to no one).
2788: The seven angels who stand before God echo Raphael's self-description as one of seven holy angels (Tob 12:15).
2789: The Sadducees' riddle of a woman married to seven brothers resembles Sarah's seven dead husbands; a likely but unproven allusion.
2790: Jesus' call to give alms and store treasure in heaven parallels Tobit 4:7-11.
2791: The deportation of northern Israel to Assyria is the historical setting Tobit assumes.
2805: Probably a Hebrew original (the Greek is full of Hebrew idioms) now lost; survives in Greek; Jerome made his Latin from an Aramaic copy.
2806: A Jewish author in Judea, probably in the Hasmonean (Maccabean) period, telling a story set in an imaginary Israel threatened by an Assyrian army.
2807:
Judith is a dramatic tale of national deliverance. The army of Holofernes, general of Nebuchadnezzar, besieges the hill town of Bethulia, which guards the way to Jerusalem. As the water runs out the elders agree to surrender in five days. Judith, a wealthy, devout widow, rebukes them for testing God, prays, dresses in her finery and goes into the enemy camp. She wins Holofernes' trust, and when he lies drunk in his tent she cuts off his head with his own sword. The leaderless army panics and flees, and Judith leads Israel in a victory song.

The book opens with what look like deliberate impossibilities: Nebuchadnezzar is called king of the Assyrians ruling in Nineveh (Nineveh fell in 612 BC, before his reign), the Temple has recently been rededicated after the return from exile, and Bethulia is otherwise unknown. Many modern scholars, including Catholic ones, read these as signals that the story is a theological novella, a composite of Israel's enemies, not a botched history. Others in older Catholic and Orthodox writing tried to fit it into real history (for example under Ashurbanipal or Artaxerxes III). Its themes echo Jael and Deborah, the Exodus song and the Maccabean struggle.
2808: A story about a brave, prayerful widow who saves her town by beheading an enemy general. It celebrates God rescuing his people through the weak. Catholics and Orthodox count it as Scripture; Jews and Protestants do not, partly because its history does not line up with what we know.
2809: Nebuchadnezzar's campaign and Holofernes' march west (ch. 1-3)
2810: Israel prepares; Achior the Ammonite warns Holofernes that Israel is protected while faithful (ch. 4-6)
2811: Siege of Bethulia and the elders' five-day deadline (ch. 7)
2813: Judith in the enemy camp and the beheading of Holofernes (ch. 10-13)
2814: Rout of the Assyrians and Judith's song of praise (ch. 14-16)
2815:
Jews: not part of the Hebrew Bible; no Hebrew text survived in Jewish use, though medieval Hebrew retellings tied it to Hanukkah. Some scholars suggest that its Hasmonean flavour or the conversion of Achior (an Ammonite, compare Deut 23:3) made it awkward, but the main reason is simply that it was outside the received collection.

Protestants: Luther found it edifying but suggested it was a sacred drama or allegory rather than history. The Reformers applied Jerome's Hebrew-canon rule and pointed to the apparent historical errors (Nebuchadnezzar as king of Assyria in Nineveh, unknown places, a garbled chronology) as evidence it was not inspired history. Some also objected to Judith's deceptive words to Holofernes being praised. Article VI lists it as readable for example but not doctrine.
2816:
Catholic and Orthodox churches received it from the Greek Old Testament. Clement of Rome held Judith up as an example of courageous faith before AD 100, and Jerome reported that the Council of Nicaea was said to have counted it among the Scriptures (which is why he translated it despite doubts). Hippo, Carthage, Trent and Jerusalem 1672 list it.

Defenders say it should be judged as the kind of writing it is: an inspired story whose truth is theological. It teaches that God saves by the hand of a woman (Jdt 9:10; 13:15), that leaders must not put God on a deadline, and that prayer, fasting and courage go together. Judith became a model of Israel itself and, for many Fathers, a figure of the Church and of Mary.
2817: Old Testament-era book; apostolicity does not apply.
2818: Probably written c. 150-100 BC, after the period Jews later regarded as the age of prophecy.
2819: Its theology of prayer and trust is orthodox; critics query praise of deception and violence (though the same question arises for Jael in Judg 4-5).
2820: Read across the Greek and Latin churches but doubted by those who followed the Hebrew list.
2821: Used by Clement of Rome, read liturgically in the East and West.
2822: Makes no prophetic claim; it is narrated anonymously.
2823: Cites Judith, alongside Esther, as a woman who risked herself to save her people.
2824: Translated Judith from Aramaic in one night, noting that the Synod of Nicaea was said to have counted it among the Scriptures.
2825: Jael killing Sisera in her tent is the clearest model for Judith's deed.
2826: Deborah's song praises Jael much as Israel praises Judith (Jdt 13:18; 15:9-10).
2827: Judith's victory song (Jdt 16) is patterned on the songs of Moses and Miriam.
2828: Achior the Ammonite is circumcised and joins Israel (Jdt 14:10), in tension with this law; a point often noted in discussions of the book.
2840: Colophon dated to 114 BC (Ptolemy VIII and Cleopatra III)
2841: Colophon dated to 78/77 BC (Ptolemy XII and Cleopatra V)
2842: Greek; two additions (the royal decrees B and E) were composed in polished Greek, while others (A, C, D, F) may go back to Hebrew or Aramaic sources.
2843: Jewish translators and editors; a colophon says the Greek Esther was brought to Egypt by Dositheus and translated by Lysimachus son of Ptolemy of Jerusalem.
2844:
The Greek version of Esther contains six blocks of material (107 verses), usually labelled A to F, that are not in the Hebrew book. A opens with Mordecai's dream of two dragons and his uncovering of a plot; B gives the text of Haman's decree to destroy the Jews; C contains long prayers of Mordecai and Esther; D expands Esther's unsummoned approach to the king, who softens when God changes his spirit; E is the king's second decree, condemning Haman; F interprets the dream and ends with a colophon about the translation.

The most striking effect is religious. The Hebrew Esther famously never names God, while the additions mention God over fifty times, add prayer, and have Esther protest that she loathes the pagan marriage bed and has not eaten at Haman's table. Jerome, translating from Hebrew, moved the additions to the end of his book, which is why Catholic Bibles once numbered them as Esther 10:4-16:24; modern Catholic Bibles put them back in their story order with letters.
2845: Extra passages found in the Greek version of Esther, adding prayers, dreams and royal letters. They make the story openly religious, since the Hebrew Esther never mentions God. Catholics and Orthodox read them as part of Esther; Jews and Protestants follow the shorter Hebrew book.
2846: A: Mordecai's dream of two dragons and the eunuchs' plot (before Esth 1:1)
2847: B: Text of the king's decree against the Jews (after Esth 3:13)
2848: C: Prayers of Mordecai and Esther (after Esth 4:17)
2849: D: Esther before the king; God changes his anger to gentleness (replacing Esth 5:1-2)
2850: E: The king's decree in favour of the Jews (after Esth 8:12)
2851: F: The dream explained and the translation colophon (after Esth 10:3)
2853:
Jews keep the Hebrew Esther, read at Purim, without these passages; they were never part of the Hebrew text.

Protestants followed Jerome, who marked them as additions found only in Greek. Since no Hebrew original was known and the decrees are plainly Greek compositions, Reformers treated them as secondary expansions. Some also noted inconsistencies with the Hebrew story (for example Haman is called a Macedonian in Addition E, and the timing of Mordecai's reward differs). Article VI lists the rest of Esther among books read but not used for doctrine.

Syriac: the Peshitta Esther follows the Hebrew and lacks the additions, hence n/a.
2854: Catholic and Orthodox churches received Esther in its Greek form as part of the Septuagint, and Trent defined the books with all their parts as they were read in the Church. For them, the additions are an inspired interpretation that makes explicit what the Hebrew leaves implicit: that God guided events and that Esther's courage rose from prayer. Esther's prayer (Addition C) has long been used in Christian devotion and liturgy. The Ethiopian tradition likewise uses the fuller Esther.
2855: Old Testament-era material; apostolicity does not apply.
2856: Added around 100 BC, later than the Hebrew Esther.
2857: Theologically conventional; it makes God's role explicit rather than introducing new teaching.
2858: Read with Esther wherever the Greek Bible was used; absent where the Hebrew or Peshitta was used.
2859: Esther's prayer was used in Christian devotion and liturgy.
2860: The additions do not claim separate authority; they present themselves as part of Esther.
2861: Recalls Esther's fasting and humbling herself before God, which fits the prayer of Addition C.
2862: Translated Esther from Hebrew and placed the Greek additions at the end, marking them as not found in the Hebrew.
2863: The Hebrew merely mentions Haman's letters; Addition B supplies their full text.
2864: Mordecai's hint that deliverance will come from another place is the closest the Hebrew comes to naming God; the additions make it explicit.
2865: Esther's call to fast is where Addition C inserts her and Mordecai's prayers.
2866: Addition E is placed here, giving the king's counter-decree.
2877: Greek, written in Greek from the start (it uses Greek rhetorical forms and philosophical terms).
2878: A learned Jew in Alexandria, Egypt, writing in the voice of King Solomon (a literary convention, not a claim most readers took literally; Jerome and Augustine knew it was not by Solomon).
2879:
Wisdom is a sustained appeal, written in the persona of Solomon, to love righteousness and seek divine Wisdom. Part one contrasts the ungodly, who think life ends at death and so oppress the righteous, with the righteous whose souls are in the hand of God and who will shine in judgement. Part two praises Wisdom herself as a breath of God's power, a pure emanation of his glory, a reflection of eternal light, and recounts Solomon's prayer for her. Part three retells the Exodus as a lesson in how God uses creation to punish the wicked and rescue the righteous, with a long critique of idolatry.

Wisdom is a bridge text. It is thoroughly Jewish yet uses Greek ideas such as the immortality of the soul and the four cardinal virtues. Its language about Wisdom and its argument that idolatry leads to immorality closely resemble passages in Paul, Hebrews and John, so many scholars think New Testament writers knew it, though none quotes it by name.
2880: A Greek-Jewish book written in Solomon's name that praises God's Wisdom, promises immortality to the righteous and mocks idol-worship. Its ideas sound very like parts of Paul and Hebrews. Catholics and Orthodox count it as Scripture; Jews and Protestants do not.
2881: The fate of the righteous and the ungodly; immortality (ch. 1-5)
2882: Solomon's search for Wisdom and portrait of Wisdom (ch. 6-9)
2883: Wisdom's work in history from Adam to the Exodus (ch. 10)
2884: The Exodus plagues as measured judgement and mercy (ch. 11-12, 16-19)
2885: The folly and origins of idolatry (ch. 13-15)
2886:
Jews: composed in Greek in Egypt and never part of the Hebrew Bible; the rabbis did not transmit it.

Protestants: the Reformers accepted Jerome's judgement that it was not by Solomon and not in the Hebrew canon, so it could not be prophetic Scripture. Luther admired it but noted its late Greek origin. Article VI places it among books read for instruction, not doctrine. Some Protestant critics also noted Greek philosophical ideas (for instance the body weighing down the soul, Wis 9:15, and pre-existent souls, Wis 8:19-20) as foreign to Hebrew thought.
2887:
It was in the Greek Bible of the early church and very widely quoted by the Fathers, from Clement of Rome onward; the Muratorian Fragment even listed it with New Testament books. Hippo, Carthage, Trent and Jerusalem 1672 all receive it.

Catholics and Orthodox prize its clear teaching on the afterlife and the judgement of the righteous (Wis 3:1-9 is read at funerals), its doctrine of Wisdom that the Fathers read as a prophecy of Christ the Wisdom and image of God, and its passage about the righteous one mocked and killed (Wis 2:12-20), which Christians read as foreshadowing the Passion. The strong verbal parallels with Romans and Hebrews are, for them, a sign that the apostles drew on it.
2888: Old Testament-era book; it claims Solomon's voice but is not apostolic or genuinely Solomonic.
2889: Written in the last century BC or early first century AD, so very close to the New Testament in time.
2890: Its theology of God, judgement and Wisdom is widely accepted; some see Greek dualism of soul and body.
2891: Universally read in the Greek and Latin churches; denied canonical status by those who followed the Hebrew list.
2892: Heavily used in early Christian preaching and liturgy.
2893: Written as Solomon's prayer and teaching, but does not claim prophetic revelation.
2894: Appears to echo Wisdom on God's power and who can resist it.
2896: Lists Wisdom, written by friends of Solomon in his honour, among books accepted in the church, in a list otherwise of New Testament books.
2897: Included it in his list of the canonical Scriptures received by the churches, while noting that books accepted by more and weightier churches should be preferred.
2898: Paul's argument that creation reveals God and idolatry is inexcusable closely follows Wisdom 13:1-9 and 14:22-27.
2899: The potter making vessels from the same clay parallels Wisdom 15:7.
2900: The Son as radiance of God's glory echoes Wisdom 7:25-26.
2901: The mockers at the cross say God should rescue him if he is God's son, as in Wisdom 2:18 (also Ps 22:8).
2902: God's armour of righteousness and the helmet of salvation recall Wisdom 5:17-20 (and Isa 59:17).
2903: Christ the power and wisdom of God draws on the personified Wisdom tradition that Wisdom of Solomon develops.
2913: Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach
2916: Hebrew original; about two-thirds recovered from Cairo Genizah manuscripts (found 1896 onward), Masada (chapters 39-44) and Qumran; translated into Greek by the author's grandson in Egypt.
2917: Jesus (Yeshua) ben Eleazar ben Sira, a Jerusalem sage and teacher, writing c. 190-175 BC; his grandson's prologue dates the Greek translation to the 38th year of Ptolemy VIII Euergetes (132 BC).
2918:
Sirach is the longest wisdom book in the Bible tradition and the only one whose author is known by name. Like Proverbs it gives practical counsel on friendship, speech, money, family, work, health and table manners, but it also ties wisdom to Israel's Law: Wisdom seeks a home among all peoples and settles in Zion, and is identified with the book of the covenant (ch. 24). It ends with a long Praise of the Fathers (ch. 44-50), from Enoch to the high priest Simon son of Onias, and a closing prayer and poem.

The grandson's prologue is a precious piece of canon history: it mentions the Law, the Prophets and the other books of the ancestors, an early witness to a three-part Hebrew scripture. Sirach was quoted with respect in the Talmud, even though rabbis also ruled it outside the sacred books. The Latin name Ecclesiasticus (the church book) reflects how much Christians used it for teaching.
2919: A book of wise sayings by a Jerusalem teacher named Jesus ben Sira, about 180 BC, covering everything from friendship to money to honouring God's Law. Rabbis quoted it but did not count it as Scripture. Catholics and Orthodox do; Protestants treat it as good reading at most.
2920: Grandson's prologue on translating and the Law, Prophets and other books
2921: Fear of the Lord as the beginning of wisdom (ch. 1-2)
2922: Practical counsel on family, speech, friendship, wealth and sin (ch. 3-23, 25-43)
2923: Wisdom's hymn: Wisdom dwells in Zion as the Law (ch. 24)
2924: Praise of creation and of the famous ancestors from Enoch to Simon the high priest (ch. 42-50)
2925: Prayer of thanks and invitation to the house of learning (ch. 51)
